what: Slider-crank linkage. One motor turns two equal-radius cranks on the same shaft through a 24:1 worm drive. A 40 mm rod and an 80 mm rod connect those cranks to two passive guided carriages. Both carriages have the same ideal 48 mm complete stroke, but they occupy different fractions of that stroke at the same crank angle. The finite experiment pauses every 45 degrees, completes one forward revolution, reverses through the same phases and returns home. The numerical values below are geometric predictions; see the packaged acceptance record for the separately measured results. try: In Robot Lab choose File → Open a model… and select models/rod-ratio.ldr. In Mat choose Plain. In the Code tab select Pseudocode, paste the complete programs/rod-ratio.bw text and choose ⇦ To blocks. Use Reset to restore the saved full-extension pose and encoder datum, then press Robot Lab Run. This isolated add-on is not automatically installed in Examples.

Watch stages 0–8 visit crank phases 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°, 180°, 225°, 270°, 315° and 360°. Stages 9–16 visit the reverse route back to 0°. Each measured arrival has a one-second dwell. The final status is completed = 1, failed = 0, stage = 17 and arrived = 0.

At the first 90° crank pause, compare each carriage with its own saved starting point. Predict which has moved farther. Ideally the short-rod carriage has moved inward 32.000 mm and the long-rod carriage 27.685 mm: a difference of 4.315 mm. Neither is halfway through its 48 mm stroke.

Compare the two 180° endpoints and the matching phases on the reverse route. Both complete strokes should be 48 mm in the ideal geometry. The different rod lengths change the intermediate position, not the crank radius or the number of cycles. Measure the actual carriage markers instead of treating a motor target as an output observation.

The displayed phaseTarget is output crank degrees. The motor turns 24 times as far: a full crank revolution requires 8640 motor degrees, with the measured sign in the supplied program. The requested 720 motor degrees per second corresponds nominally to 30 crank degrees per second between pauses. Reset before a fresh run after any manual movement or interrupted experiment.
why: For an inline slider-crank, let r be the crank radius, L the rod length and θ the crank angle from full extension. The crank tip has coordinates (r cos θ, r sin θ). The carriage stays on the straight guide line, so the rod supplies the remaining horizontal distance sqrt(L² − r² sin² θ). Its pivot position is x_L = r cos θ + sqrt(L² − r² sin² θ). Inward travel from its own full-extension position is u_L = r + L − x_L. At 0° and 180° the sine term vanishes, making the complete stroke exactly 2r for either rod. Between those angles, the shorter rod has the larger angular swing and the larger departure from the simple cosine projection. Here r = 24 mm, with L = 40 mm and L = 80 mm.
matters: A single input can give two passive outputs the same endpoints and different motion within the cycle. That distinction matters when matching a carriage to another mechanism: equal stroke and equal cycle count do not guarantee equal position at each phase. The common shaft provides the same crank phase to both branches, while two real guide rails restrain each carriage. This experiment concerns displacement, phase and geometric closure. It does not establish motor torque, joint friction, efficiency, wear or a physical load rating.
question: If both cranks have a 24 mm radius, must their carriages also have the same position halfway through a crank half-turn? Does doubling the connecting-rod length double the complete stroke?
answer: No to both. At a 90° crank angle, the 40 mm rod gives 32.000 mm of inward travel and the 80 mm rod gives about 27.685 mm. Doubling the rod length reduces the intermediate distortion but leaves the complete stroke at 2 × 24 = 48 mm. A longer rod approaches the cosine-projection motion; it does not increase the crank radius.
further: Calculate the two ideal travels at 45° and 135°, then compare them with independent marker measurements. Subtract each carriage’s own saved point so the rods’ different absolute starting positions do not become a false difference.

Compare 90° with 270° and compare matching forward and reverse phases. The ideal displacement equation gives the same position for θ and 360° − θ. A disagreement in measured runs needs investigation; it is not part of the ideal rod-length effect.

Compare Quickstroke, whose guide line is offset from its crank centre, with this inline arrangement. Quickstroke studies unequal stroke times; Rod Ratio deliberately pauses to compare positions at common phases.

Identify the 24 mm crank radius and the 40 mm and 80 mm distances between rod pivot centres. Count hole intervals, not the number of holes. Then inspect the guide supports and collars that keep each slider and shaft captive.
formula: r = 24 mm; L_short = 40 mm; L_long = 80 mm; N = 24. x_L(θ) = r cos θ + sqrt(L² − r² sin² θ); u_L(θ) = r + L − x_L(θ). Stroke = 2r = 48 mm. u_short(90°) = 32.000 mm; u_long(90°) ≈ 27.684864 mm; difference ≈ 4.315136 mm. Output crank angle in degrees = measured_sign × unwrapped_motor_angle / 24. The curve observer uses the actual crank marker angle independently of that encoder prediction.
